name: TRL Scale Explained
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Nine Steps From Idea to Working Machine
lesson.summary: Walking through all nine technology readiness levels in order shows exactly how large the gap is between an early laboratory result and a proven, operational system, a gap that gets collapsed in most popular coverage of new technology.
lesson.body:
Building on Technology Readiness Levels, it helps to walk through what each of the nine levels concretely requires, because the gap between adjacent levels is not uniform, some are small engineering steps and others represent years of extra work and entirely new categories of risk. TRL 1 is basic principles observed, a phenomenon reported in the scientific literature with no application yet in view. TRL 2 is technology concept formulated, a specific practical application proposed on paper, building on that principle. TRL 3 is experimental proof of concept, a lab experiment validating that the concept can actually work, typically in a highly controlled, simplified setting far removed from real world conditions.

TRL 4 is validation in a laboratory environment, individual components integrated and tested together as a system on a bench under favorable, controlled conditions. TRL 5 is validation in a relevant environment, those components tested together in conditions that start to resemble real use, higher fidelity than a pure lab setup but not yet the final application. TRL 6, the important midpoint, is demonstration in a relevant environment, a full representative prototype built and tested under conditions close to actual operation. Reaching TRL 6 is often where a technology starts looking credible to non specialist investors and customers, since it is the first level involving something close to a complete, working system rather than isolated components tested in isolation.

TRL 7 is demonstration in an operational environment, an actual prototype tested in the real final setting. TRL 8 is system complete and qualified, the final form technology tested and proven. TRL 9 is proven through successful operations, genuinely deployed and doing its real job repeatedly in production. A jet engine illustrates this well: a novel combustion technique might sit at TRL 3 when first proven on a lab rig, reach TRL 6 when a full scale prototype runs on a test stand mimicking flight, and only reach TRL 9 after years more testing, once it is powering commercial aircraft on regular routes.

The width of the gap between TRL 3 and TRL 9 is the central lesson here. A TRL 3 lab result, however scientifically impressive, genuinely proving that a physical effect exists and can be harnessed, is often five, six, or more years and enormous additional engineering investment away from TRL 9, and there is no guarantee every promising TRL 3 result successfully makes that entire climb. Media coverage and company press releases often describe TRL 3 or TRL 4 results using the same confident, forward looking language usually reserved for TRL 8 or TRL 9 achievements, which is exactly the confusion the TRL scale was invented to prevent.

With the full ladder in view, the next concept applies it directly to quantum computing hardware, and argues most current approaches sit much lower on it than the surrounding narrative suggests.
